newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Lili increases in strength as it lashes Bahamas.
newsitem.headline: Lili increases in strength as it lashes Bahamas.

text.p: Hurricane Lili strengthened to a Category 2 storm as it lashed the central Bahamas early on Saturday after dumping torrential rain on Cuba.
Flooding from the storm was blamed for 10 deaths in Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica earlier in the week but there were no reports of deaths in Cuba, officials said.
At 5 a.m. EDT (0800 GMT), Lili was packing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), making it a Category 2 hurricane, according to forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami.

The storm was located 40 miles (65 km) southeast of San Salvador island at latitude 23.9 north and longitude 75.1 west. It picked up speed from a cold front moving across Florida and swirled east at 23 mph (37 kph), crossing Great Exuma island with heavy rains and strong winds.
"It's strengthened a little bit since moving off the Cuban coast and it's moving a little faster," said Andrew Shashy, a forecaster at the hurricane center.

The central portion of the Bahamas, an archipelego of hundreds of islands stretching more than 600 miles (950 km) in the Atlantic, lay in the path of Lili, which was expected to finish crossing the chain later on Saturday morning.

On San Salvador, a small Bahamian island that claims to be the first place in the New World where explorer Christopher Columbus stepped foot in 1492, residents tied up sailboats on Saturday and secured diving equipment ahead of Lili's arrival.
The 25-mile-long (40 km) island is home to 700 residents and a Club Med beach resort.
"A few people here may be worried, but not me. Every year they (hurricanes) come close but they never hit us directly," said Dwight Johnson, 25, a resident bartender said Saturday.

Some tourists at the resort expressed concern, but others crowded into the resort's casino to get their minds off the rainy weather and howling winds that preceded Lili's arrival. "Better a hurricane in the Caribbean than rain or snow in Berlin," said Detlev Freutel, a 45-year-old German tourist.

Hurricane warnings remained in effect for the northwest and central Bahamas from Andros island southward and eastward, including the capital city of Nassau and Long Island, Cat Island, Eleuthera Island, Great Exuma Island, Andros Island and San Salvador.

Schools closed early on Friday in the Bahamas, flights were canceled and customers crowded into food stores and gasoline stations to gather supplies for the storm. Some tourist hotels handed out candles in case electricity failed during the storm.

Wind gusts of up to 115 (180 kmh) were clocked in central Cuba on Friday when Lili slammed across the island, peeling off roofs, flooding coastal homes and causing at least 20 houses to collapse in the city of Matanzas, the state news agency AIN said.
The strongest winds of the storm passed to the east of the capital Havana. State radio said about 75,000 people were evacuated from crumbling and decaying buildings in Havana as a precaution.
The national civil defense organization said some 7,000 homes were partially or completely damaged in central and western provinces. Most had damaged roofs but 130 homes were completely ruined.
Some 53 homes in Havana partially collapsed, most of them in the city's historic quarter where many old buildings are in a state of decay.
Lili dumped torrential rain of up to 12 inches (30 cm) in its path, sending rivers over their banks and causing flash flooding.

President Fidel Castro echoed the feelings of Havana's two million inhabitants when he told reporters that while things might be bad, at least the "worst scenario" had not happened -- Hurricane Lili passing over the capital.

Although Florida dodged the hurricane, Cuban exiles in Miami went on Spanish-language radio stations asking for donations of rice, beans, baby food and other non-perishable items to send to Cuba. A Catholic charity also began collecting cash donations intended for the communist-ruled island, whose economy has been struggling since the collapse of the former Soviet Union.
Relieved residents of Key West opened up storm shutters on Friday afternoon after it became apparent that the Florida Keys would be spared the worst of Lili.
